name: J. H. Kinzie's Store
aka: John H. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant

documented_range.note: THE DATES ARE THE BUSINESS'S AND NOT THE BUILDING'S. Andreas lists 'Jim Kinzie's store, P. F. W. Peck's store, Harmon's and Loomis's' as all being on South Water Street by 1833, and separately records J. H. Kinzie advertising as a forwarding and commission merchant in 1834. The range opens at the start of 1833 on the first of those and closes at the end of the scene year on the ordinary continuity cut. Nothing reached dates the BUILDING at either end. A NAME CAUTION THAT AFFECTS NOTHING GEOMETRIC BUT SHOULD TRAVEL WITH THE RECORD: Andreas's 'Jim Kinzie' is James Kinzie, who kept the Wolf Point Tavern and the Green Tree on the west bank, while the 1834 forwarding advertisements are John H. Kinzie's. Whether the South Water store belonged to one brother, the other, or both at different times is not settled by anything reached, and the id follows the initials Andreas uses in the advertisement rather than the nickname he uses in the list.

position.symbolic_location: South side of South Water Street between Franklin Street and Wells Street (today the south side of West Wacker Drive) — the street is attested, the block is not.
position.note: CONJECTURAL, AND ONLY THE STREET IS EVIDENCE. Andreas puts this store 'on South Water Street' and no closer; this project's dossier records the block as unattested. The point recorded here is on the south side of the Franklin-to-Wells block, and the choice of block carries ONE weak argument and no more: a forwarding and commission house wants wharfage, and the west end of South Water was the wharf and landing end nearest the forks and the South Branch, so the west end is a slightly better guess than the east. That is a reason, not evidence, and it is the difference between this record and a coin toss rather than the difference between a guess and a finding. THE ALONG-STREET UNCERTAINTY IS THE WHOLE STREET, about 630 m from Market to State. THE SIDE OF THE STREET IS REASONED: the north side of South Water was the river bank, wharves and landings (docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 12), so a store building is on the south side, however much its trade faced the water. METHOD, for the cross-street position only: the modern West Upper Wacker Drive centreline was interpolated between the intersection centres at North Franklin (EPSG:26916 E 447281.2, N 4637407.2) and North Wells (E 447402.5, N 4637411.6), read from OpenStreetMap 2026-08-11, and the south kerb taken 12.2 m south of it as half an 80 ft platted street. Working uncertainty about 20 m across the street from the georeference (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS) and the length of the street along it. Facade bearing 0, north onto South Water, inferred from the street rather than from any statement.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: INVENTED — the parcel's borrowed rectangle, 12.192 x 7.62 m = 40 x 25 ft, from the Green Tree Tavern's attested frontage and room module. Nothing is attested about this building. The larger rather than the smaller rectangle is used because a forwarding and commission house handles other men's goods and needs floor for them, which is an argument about the trade and not about the building. The documented South Water lot width of 55 ft is a cap and 40 ft sits inside it.

stories.note: Nothing is attested. One is recorded because it is the smaller claim, though a forwarding house with a loft over would be as likely. Invention, tagged as such.

construction.note: Not stated. Frame rather than log because a store house wants clear floor and wide doors, and because this project's dossier records the mid-1830s South Water commercial stock as frame. Braced rather than balloon frame follows the Sauganash record's argument.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.6 m is about 12 ft: one storey built taller than a dwelling's, which is what stacked goods and a cart door need. It inherits the storey count's uncertainty, which is conjectural.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for this building. 33 degrees is the frame_storefront archetype's own figure for a store, and it is adopted here rather than the 38 this project uses for taverns because the archetype argues the case from the dataset's one attested store footprint: a store's frontage is long and its plan shallow, so a tavern's pitch puts more roof above the eave than there is wall below it and the building stops reading as a shop. Inferred from construction practice and from the type, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the minimum for premises worked through Chicago winters. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

phases.change_note: A Kinzie store on South Water Street, one of the three Andreas names as being there by 1833, trading as a forwarding and commission house in 1834 — the business of taking other men's goods off the schooners and getting them inland, which is what South Water Street was for.

function.note: Andreas records J. H. Kinzie advertising as a forwarding and commission merchant in 1834 and separately lists a Kinzie store among those on South Water Street by 1833. The trade is documented; which building held it is not.

occupants.value: J. H. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant
occupants.note: Inferred rather than documented because of the name question set out on documented_range: Andreas's list says 'Jim Kinzie's store' and his 1834 advertisement says J. H. Kinzie, and those are two different men of the same family. The record follows the advertisement because an advertisement is the man's own word about his own business, and flags the doubt rather than resolving it.

research_note: A DOCUMENTED TRADE ON AN UNDOCUMENTED LOT. Andreas puts a Kinzie store on South Water Street by 1833 and records J. H. Kinzie advertising as a forwarding and commission merchant in 1834, and gives no block, no corner, no description and no dimension. Position and footprint are conjectural and storeys with them; only the trade and the street survive as evidence. TWO THINGS IN THIS RECORD ARE WORTH THE NEXT READER'S ATTENTION. FIRST, THE NAME: 'Jim Kinzie' is James Kinzie of Wolf Point, who already appears in this dataset as the builder of the Wolf Point Tavern and the Green Tree, while the forwarding advertisements are John H. Kinzie's. The record follows the advertisement and says so. SECOND, THE BLOCK CHOICE carries a weak trade argument — forwarding wants wharfage, and the west end of South Water was the landing end — which is stated on the position so that it can be overturned by one line of evidence rather than defended. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE IT: any 1834-35 Chicago Democrat advertisement carrying the store's address, which is very likely to exist since Andreas is quoting from those files; or the 1834-35 town lot records for South Water. See docs/RESEARCH/jh_kinzie_forwarding_store.md.
